conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in because of weakness and falls at home, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve fallen eight times since I got home. I just feel so weak. No dizziness or passing out, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your cough has been getting worse too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, dry and persistent. No fever, but it’s tiring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your CT chest from today. It shows your lung infection has worsened since your last hospitalization. We’re concerned about multifocal pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I just finished antibiotics. What kind of infection is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Your sputum showed Pseudomonas, which is resistant to some antibiotics. We’ll do a bronchoscopy to get a better sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s important to find out exactly what’s in your lungs so we can treat it properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative, which is good—no active bloodstream infection right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the bronchoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow. We also got your CT head—no bleeding or fracture. Your falls are likely due to weakness, not a brain issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the bronchoscopy. The lavage showed yeast and gram-positive rods. We’re starting you on voriconazole for possible fungal infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fungal? I thought it was bacterial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be both. Your immune system is weak, so you’re at risk for multiple infections. The yeast might be related to your immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the Pseudomonas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s resistant to ceftazidime, so we’re switching to ciprofloxacin. We’ll give it for eight days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI pelvis and spine are back. No new spinal issues or abscess. The weakness is likely from deconditioning and steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroid use? You mean from my transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, prednisone can cause muscle weakness over time. We’ll work on rehab to help rebuild strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fungal culture confirmed yeast. We’re increasing your voriconazole dose to better fight it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We adjusted your tacrolimus dose too, since voriconazole can raise its levels. We’ll monitor that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed blood in your ostomy bag. That’s new. We’re ordering a CT abdomen to check for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Could that be serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. Given your history, we’re worried about varices—swollen veins from liver issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows cirrhosis and varices around your colostomy. That’s likely where the bleeding is coming from.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cirrhosis? I don’t drink. How did I get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely nonalcoholic—possibly from fatty liver disease related to diabetes, or from medication or transplant effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need a TIPS procedure—transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt. It reduces pressure in those veins and stops bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well during the TIPS. They placed a stent and embolized the bleeding varices. The pressure in your liver dropped significantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from those veins. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’re now on ciprofloxacin to prevent infection around the shunt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your galactomannan test came back positive. That confirms the fungal infection in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the voriconazole is the right choice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re keeping you on the higher dose. Your breathing is improving, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver biopsy confirmed cirrhosis and bile duct damage. Likely due to medication or graft-versus-host disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage it. You’ll follow up with hepatology. The TIPS should help prevent more bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CBC is stable. We were worried about pancytopenia, but your donor cells are still engrafted—no rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my counts are okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re low but stable. We’ll keep monitoring. No need for transfusions now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows your TIPS is working well—good blood flow through the shunt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means the pressure is reduced and you’re protected from more bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cough is better, and your oxygen levels are normal. You’re breathing on room air without trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger too. When can I go to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging it. You’ll go to inpatient rehab for up to 30 days to build strength and prevent falls.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sacral ulcer is clean—no infection. Keep using the special mattress and we’ll continue wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s stable. MRI showed no bone infection, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test was negative, so we can stop the isolation precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I hate the gloves and gowns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re wrapping up your ciprofloxacin for pneumonia. You’ll stay on it daily for shunt protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the voriconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue that twice daily until your infectious disease follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your TIPS is patent, lungs are clearer, and no more bleeding. You’re strong enough for rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so relieved. What about my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your insulin. Try to stick to a consistent carb diet—Glucerna shakes can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to rehab. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Follow up with your specialists, and call if you have any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Rehab team will meet you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to get stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right path. Keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.
